analysis.one_liner: Makes large internet platforms and broadband providers help pay for rural and low-income connectivity programs.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by six senators including one Democrat, never got a hearing or vote in the Senate Commerce Committee and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Right now, the federal fund that pays for phone and internet service in rural areas, schools, libraries, and low-income households is financed almost entirely by a fee that telephone companies pass on to their customers. This bill would have directed the FCC to make big broadband providers and large internet companies — search engines, social media, streaming, cloud and e-commerce firms — contribute to that fund, spreading the cost so the fee on ordinary phone bills could shrink. It would also create a dedicated subsidy for one broadband provider per hard-to-serve rural area. The bill never advanced past committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who pay the Universal Service Fund fee on their phone and internet bills, low-income Lifeline recipients, rural residents who need subsidized broadband, schools, libraries, and rural health clinics that rely on the fund.

how_it_helps.text: Expands the Universal Service Fund's contribution base so large broadband and edge providers pay in, instead of the cost falling almost entirely on telephone companies and their customers [S2].
Exempts only small platforms — those under 3% of U.S. broadband data traffic and under $5 billion in U.S. revenue — so the largest tech companies bear the new obligation [S3].
Requires the FCC to build a stable funding mechanism so broadband providers serving rural high-cost areas get support for costs that user rates and existing subsidies cannot cover [S2].
The Universal Service Fund supports rural connectivity, schools and libraries, rural health care, and the Lifeline program that discounts phone and internet service for low-income consumers [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large internet platforms — search engines, social media, streaming, cloud, app stores and e-commerce — and large broadband providers, which would face a new contribution obligation; some cost could be passed to consumers in prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big tech platforms and broadband companies

drawbacks.text: The new USF contributions are not free money: large platforms and broadband companies may pass some of the cost through to consumers in the form of higher prices or fees [S3].
The new high-cost subsidy is limited to one eligible carrier per area, which locks in a single subsidized provider for each region rather than fostering competition among rural providers [S3].
The bill gives the FCC no new regulatory authority over broadband providers or edge providers beyond the contribution requirement, so it does nothing about underlying broadband prices [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers the trade is favorable: the fee that today sits almost entirely on telephone customers would be spread across the biggest tech companies and broadband providers, easing the per-household charge while preserving funding for rural and low-income service. The main costs are potential price pass-through by large platforms and a new single-carrier rural subsidy that entrenches incumbents rather than testing competition. The bill is modest — it does not regulate broadband prices or address why service is expensive — but it is a real improvement to how a pro-consumer fund is financed.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate bill was read twice and referred to the Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced November 15, 2023 by Sen. Mullin with original cosponsors including Sen. Kelly and Sen. Crapo, and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S1].
Six senators cosponsored the bill — five Republicans and one Democrat — but no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled [S4].
The only recorded action after introduction was the committee referral; the 118th Congress ended January 3, 2025 with the bill still in committee [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large internet platforms and broadband companies that would have owed new Universal Service Fund contributions are better off because the bill died. Ordinary phone and internet customers continue to carry the fund's costs through their bills.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big tech platforms and broadband companies

industries.industry: Large internet platforms (search, social media, streaming, cloud, e-commerce)
industries.note: The bill would require platforms that transmit large volumes of data or earn over $5 billion in U.S. revenue to help fund the Universal Service Fund, a cost they currently avoid. Keeping the fund on telephone-company fees means consumers pay it instead.
They would face a new USF contribution obligation, but would also gain a dedicated, predictable subsidy for serving rural high-cost areas that existing rates and programs cannot cover.
The bill creates a new permanent high-cost support mechanism limited to one carrier per area, locking in a single subsidized provider for each region while guaranteeing funding for rural service.
They currently bear nearly the entire USF contribution and pass it to customers; adding broadband and edge providers would relieve them of a portion of the charge on their customers' bills.
